_note: 9 Nov 2026. Games for Sentence Types. spot: which kind of sentence is it? 'tell' is the part of the sentence that gives it away (highlighted after the answer). upgrade: join or rewrite to a B2 structure; the first option is the right one, each wrong one carries the reason it is wrong.

spot.s: I missed the bus, so I walked to school.
spot.why: Two full sentences joined by so.

spot.s: Although it was raining, we played the match.
spot.why: Although it was raining cannot stand alone: it hangs on the main clause.

spot.s: My cousin from Lisbon plays the guitar in a band.
spot.why: One subject, one verb. From Lisbon and in a band are only phrases.

spot.s: When the film ended, everyone clapped, and we went for pizza.
spot.why: A when clause hangs on two full sentences joined by and.

spot.s: The phone that I bought last week has stopped working.
spot.why: A relative clause sits inside the main sentence.

spot.s: We wanted to go to the beach; however, the weather was awful.
spot.why: Two full sentences, joined by a semicolon and however.

spot.s: After school, my friends and I usually go to the park.
spot.why: After school is a phrase with no verb, so there is only one clause.

spot.s: If you leave now, you'll catch the train, but you'll have to run.
spot.why: An if clause, then two full sentences joined by but.

spot.s: Despite the noise, I finished my essay.
spot.why: Despite takes a noun, not a clause, so the sentence has only one verb.

spot.s: Having finished my homework, I went out with friends.
spot.why: Having + past participle: one action finished before the next.

spot.s: The new sports centre was opened by the mayor.
spot.why: Be + past participle: the centre receives the action.

spot.s: Never have I seen such a crowded beach.
spot.why: Never moves to the front, so have comes before I.

spot.s: What I really need is a long holiday.
spot.why: What … is splits the sentence to point at a long holiday.

spot.s: If I had known about the party, I would have gone.
spot.why: Third conditional: if + had done, would have done.

spot.s: Walking along the beach, we found a message in a bottle.
spot.why: An -ing clause: we were walking when we found it.

spot.s: It was my brother who broke the window.
spot.why: It was … who points at my brother, not anyone else.

spot.s: Had we left earlier, we would have caught the ferry.
spot.why: A conditional without if: had comes first.

spot.s: My bike has been stolen.
spot.why: Has been + past participle: we don't know who stole it.

spot.s: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the record.
spot.why: Not only at the front, so did comes before she.

spot.s: The essay, written in a hurry, was full of mistakes.
spot.why: A past participle clause adds information about the essay.

spot.s: Unless you practise, you won't improve.
spot.why: Unless means if not.

spot.s: I saved money so that I could buy a new phone.
spot.why: So that + could: the reason I saved.

spot.s: The film was so boring that I fell asleep.
spot.why: So + adjective + that: what happened because of it.

spot.s: Owing to the strike, the trains were cancelled.
spot.why: Owing to + noun gives the reason.

spot.s: Even though she was tired, she kept running.
spot.why: She kept running in spite of being tired.

spot.s: My sister loves horror films, whereas I can't stand them.
spot.why: Whereas sets two people side by side.

spot.s: In addition to playing football, he does karate.
spot.why: In addition to + -ing adds a second activity.

upgrade.from: It was raining. We played the match.

o.t: Although it was raining, we played the match.
Despite it was raining, we played the match.
o.why: Despite takes a noun or -ing: despite the rain.

o.t: Although it was raining, but we played the match.
o.why: Although and but together: one linker is enough.

upgrade.from: I finished my homework. Then I went out.

o.t: Having finished my homework, I went out.
Having finished my homework, my friends called me.
o.why: This says your friends finished your homework. The subject must be I.

o.t: Finished my homework, I went out.
o.why: You need having + past participle for the earlier action.

upgrade.from: My cousin lives in London. She is a nurse.

o.t: My cousin, who lives in London, is a nurse.
My cousin, which lives in London, is a nurse.
o.why: Which is for things. For people, use who.

o.t: My cousin who she lives in London is a nurse.
o.why: Who already is the subject, so she is not needed.

upgrade.from: Someone stole my bike last night.

o.t: My bike was stolen last night.
My bike was stole last night.
o.why: The passive needs the past participle: stolen.

o.t: My bike has stolen last night.
o.why: This says the bike stole something. And last night needs the past simple.

upgrade.from: I didn't know about the party. I didn't go.

o.t: If I had known about the party, I would have gone.
If I would have known about the party, I would have gone.
o.why: No would in the if clause: if I had known.

o.t: If I knew about the party, I would have gone.
o.why: The past needs had known, not knew.

o.t: What I need is more sleep.
What I need it is more sleep.
o.why: What already refers to the thing, so it is not needed.

o.t: That I need is more sleep.
o.why: A cleft starts with What, not That.

upgrade.from: I have never seen such a crowded beach.

o.t: Never have I seen such a crowded beach.
Never I have seen such a crowded beach.
o.why: After Never at the front, the auxiliary comes before the subject: have I.

o.t: Never have seen I such a crowded beach.
o.why: Only the auxiliary moves. The main verb stays after the subject.

upgrade.from: She saved money. She wanted to buy a new phone.

o.t: She saved money so that she could buy a new phone.
She saved money for to buy a new phone.
o.why: For to is never correct. Use to, in order to or so that.

o.t: She saved money so as she could buy a new phone.
o.why: So as is followed by to: so as to buy.

upgrade.from: The hotel was expensive. The rooms were small.

o.t: The hotel was expensive; moreover, the rooms were small.
The hotel was expensive, moreover the rooms were small.
o.why: A comma cannot join two sentences. Use a full stop or a semicolon before moreover.

o.t: The hotel was expensive moreover, the rooms were small.
o.why: The first sentence needs to end before moreover.

upgrade.goal: Show the result with so … that
upgrade.from: The film was very boring. I fell asleep.

o.t: The film was so boring that I fell asleep.
The film was such boring that I fell asleep.
o.why: Such goes with a noun (such a boring film). With an adjective alone, use so.

o.t: The film was so boring so I fell asleep.
o.why: So … that, not so … so.

upgrade.from: She won the race. She also broke the record.

o.t: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the record.
Not only she won the race, but she also broke the record.
o.why: Not only at the front needs inversion: did she win.

o.t: Not only did she won the race, but she also broke the record.
o.why: After did, use the base form: win.

upgrade.from: You won't improve if you don't practise.

o.t: Unless you practise, you won't improve.
Unless you don't practise, you won't improve.
o.why: Unless already means if not, so don't is doubled.

o.t: Unless you will practise, you won't improve.
o.why: No will after unless, just as after if.
